name: I'M GONNA GET YOUR SUCCOTASH BURGER

recipe.history:
Succotash is one of the oldest dishes in North America, with roots stretching back centuries before European contact. The word itself comes from the Narragansett language — msickquatash — meaning "boiled whole kernels of corn." The Narragansett people of present-day New England, along with many other Indigenous nations, cultivated the celebrated "Three Sisters" — corn, beans, and squash — as companion plants that supported one another in the soil. Succotash, at its most elemental, was a practical and deeply nutritious marriage of corn and shell beans, often simmered together in a clay pot over an open fire. It was sustenance, ceremony, and ingenuity all at once. When English colonists arrived and struggled to survive their first winters, it was this dish — taught to them by the very people whose land they were occupying — that kept them alive.

Over the centuries, succotash migrated south and west, morphing as it moved. In the antebellum South, enslaved cooks transformed it into something richer, adding butter, cream, and whatever vegetables were at hand — okra, peppers, tomatoes. By the early twentieth century, succotash had become a fixture of American home cooking, appearing in church cookbooks and school cafeteria trays from Maine to Mississippi. Its transition from stew to burger topping was perhaps inevitable: the natural sweetness of corn, the earthy creaminess of lima beans, and the occasional pop of a summer vegetable are exactly the kinds of bright, contrasting flavors that cut through the richness of a beef patty. A good succotash topping does what a great condiment always does — it doesn't compete with the meat, it completes it.

I remember the first time I put succotash on a burger. It was late August, the tail end of sweet corn season, and I had a cast iron skillet going on a back burner with the last ears of the year, cut fresh off the cob, hissing in brown butter alongside a handful of lima beans I'd shelled that morning. My daughter walked into the kitchen, looked at the pan, looked at the patties resting on the board, and said, "you're not putting that on a burger." I said nothing. I plated it, slid it across the counter to her, and watched her take one bite. She didn't say anything either. She just ate. That is the whole story. That is always the whole story with food that works.

A burger is only as good as the respect you give the patty, and respecting the patty means pulling it off the heat at medium rare — an internal temperature of 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, or 54 to 57 degrees Celsius. At that temperature, the center is warm and rosy, the fat has rendered just enough to coat your palate without overwhelming it, and the beef tastes like beef — grassy, mineral, alive. Well-done is a choice, but it is not a philosophy. Medium rare is a commitment to the idea that the animal gave something, and that something deserves to arrive at the table at its finest. The succotash on this burger is vibrant and sweet. It needs a patty that can hold its own. Medium rare is the only answer.
ingredients: 1 tablespoon neutral oil (such as canola or grapeseed)
2 tablespoons unsalted butter, softened (for toasting buns)
2 cups fresh or frozen corn kernels (about 3 ears if fresh)
1 cup fresh or frozen lima beans (thawed if frozen)
1/3 cup red bell pepper, finely diced
Salt and black pepper to taste
instructions: 1. Divide the ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 6 oz / 170g each). Gently form each portion into a patty roughly 3/4-inch thick, pressing a shallow dimple into the center of each with your thumb to prevent doming during cooking. Season both sides generously with kosher salt, black pepper, and garlic powder. Set aside at room temperature for 20–30 minutes before cooking.

2. If using fresh corn, shuck the ears and cut the kernels off the cob by standing each ear upright in a wide bowl and slicing downward with a sharp knife. Scrape the back of the knife along the cob to collect the milky corn liquid — add this to the kernels.
3. Cook the lima beans: if using fresh shell beans, simmer in salted water for 10–15 minutes until just tender. If using frozen, thaw completely and pat dry.

4. Make the succotash: Heat a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the butter and olive oil. Once the butter foams and subsides, add the diced red onion and red bell pepper. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 3–4 minutes until softened. Add the minced garlic and cook for 1 minute more until fragrant.

5. Add the corn kernels (with any collected liquid) to the skillet. Cook over medium-high heat without stirring for 2 minutes to develop light char and caramelization, then stir and cook for another 2 minutes. Add the lima beans and cherry tomatoes, stirring to combine. Cook for 2–3 minutes until the tomatoes just begin to soften.

6. Remove the succotash from heat. Stir in the fresh thyme, parsley, and apple cider vinegar. Season with salt and black pepper to taste. Set aside — the succotash can be served warm or at room temperature.
7. Heat a cast iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat until it begins to smoke lightly. Add the neutral oil and swirl to coat.

8. Place the patties in the skillet without pressing down. Cook for 3–4 minutes on the first side, undisturbed, until a deep brown crust forms. Flip once. Immediately lay a slice of sharp white cheddar on each patty.

9. Cook the second side for 2–3 minutes. Begin checking internal temperature after 2 minutes using an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of the patty. Remove patties from heat when they reach 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Tent loosely with foil and rest for 3–5 minutes — carryover cooking will bring the final temperature to approximately 135°F (57°C).
10. While the patties rest, toast the brioche buns: spread the cut sides with softened butter and place face-down on the same skillet over medium heat for 1–2 minutes until golden brown.

11. Assemble the burgers: spread mayonnaise on both the top and bottom buns. Place a leaf of butter lettuce on the bottom bun, followed by the rested patty with melted cheddar. Spoon a generous portion of succotash directly over the cheese, letting it cascade over the sides. Add sliced dill pickles. Cap with the top bun.
